Tinkerbug Robotics Issue #491 Bench report 21 Aug 2026

Hobby Grade GNSS Receiver Altitude and Speed Limits for High Performance Rockets

Five hobby-grade GNSS receivers were flown against identical simulated rocket trajectories to find where each one stops publishing state updates. Receivers are typically limited to 'COCOM' limits which come from a Cold War international agreement to place limits on GNSS receivers and keep them from being used in ballistic missile guidance. Limits were originally 18 km and 515 m/s. The 18 km limit seems to have been removed more recently in favor of a 600 m/s limit from the Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR Annex Handbook 2017, Section 11.A.3). Receivers still implement limits differently and generally still implement altitude limits, sometimes wildly different from the MTCR limit. The purpose of this work was to characterize the actual performance using a software-defined radio to inject simulated trajectories into several readily available inexpensive receivers.

Five parts were measured

01The gates

Every receiver here was flown against the same two trajectories through the same signal generator. If those two trajectories did not fully characterize the limits, then additional excursions were run. The top-level summary of the results is included in this table.

Measured gates, by receiver
Receiver Path Velocity gate Altitude gate Limits combined Re-open latency
SkyTraq PX1125R conducted 515 m/s 80 km independent 0.0-1.5 s
u-blox SAM-M10Q radiated, Faraday cage 515 m/s 80 km independent 0.0-1.1 s
u-blox ZED-F9P (ArduSimple) conducted 515 m/s 80 km † independent 0.1-1.0 s
Air530 (AT6558R) conducted none to 900 m/s 10 km ‡ n/a -- no velocity gate n/a
u-blox NEO-M8T conducted 515 m/s 50 km § independent 0.9-3.1 s

 Results are rounded slightly here for the purpose of summarizing. The measured brackets are given per receiver below, and in results/receivers.json.

†Slow to close: this part held a fix 2-3 s past the limit on both flights, about 400-600 m of overshoot above 80 km with position still being published. The threshold itself is normal.

‡Not an export gate. This ceiling sits below the COCOM altitude, and the receiver stops publishing there for reasons unrelated to export control.

§The u-blox dynamic model's own altitude ceiling, not an export gate. Airborne <4 g is specified at 50,000 m; no u-blox model goes higher, so this part's export behaviour above it cannot be measured.

What the table says

Receivers do not implement the current MTCR 600 m/s limit. Most use the COCOM 515 m/s limit for speed, and altitude limits vary significantly from 10 km to 80 km, though several use the 80 km limit.

02How this was measured

A HackRF One drives a simulated GPS L1 C/A constellation into each receiver through a fixed attenuator chain — conducted, never radiated, except for the flight computer's receiver which is fed by a quarter-wave inside a Faraday cage. The baseband comes from gps-sdr-sim against real broadcast ephemeris, so the satellites are where they actually were on the day.

Blocked is not the same as lost

The whole measurement rests on one distinction. A receiver that has been gated keeps tracking satellites and simply declines to publish a position; a receiver that has lost signal loses the satellites first. Every capture therefore records both the fix state and the per-satellite carrier-to-noise ratio, and each epoch is classified:

VerdictFixSatellitesMeaning
FIXyestrackedpublishing normally
BLOCKEDnostill trackedwithholding — a gate
NO_LOCKnogonelost the signal — not a gate

A result is only reported as a gate when the satellites stayed. Where a receiver was starved — fewer than four satellites through a wait — the analysis says so rather than quoting a latency.

The two standard trajectories

Every receiver flies both. They reach the same 82.5 km apogee and cross the same limits; only the boost differs, and that difference is the point.

ScenarioBoostPeak speedApogeePurpose
spaceshot15 g1343 m/s82.5 kmrealistic high-power flight; hardest case for tracking
gentle_alt3 g997 m/s82.5 kmsame envelope crossed slowly — this is what brackets the thresholds

Why two. At a 1 Hz navigation rate a 15 g boost covers 118 m/s between one epoch and the next, so a fast flight can only ever bracket the velocity gate coarsely no matter how carefully it is flown. The 3 g ascent crosses the same threshold slowly enough to pin it. Both are integrated from thrust, drag and gravity rather than drawn as ramps, and flown to the ground under a drogue-then-main recovery.

Each flight opens with a 180 s pad hold so the receiver has acquired and settled before anything moves. Trajectory time is recovered from the GPS time in the receiver's own output, so no clock synchronisation between the transmitter and the analysis is needed.

One signal, one band. The injection is GPS L1 C/A only. Every receiver here is multi-constellation and two are multi-band, so all of them are being tested well below what they can do. That is a property of the rig, not of any part, and it applies equally to all five — which is what makes the comparison fair even though it is not representative of open-sky performance.

03Receiver by receiver

The same two profiles, part by part. Each pair of plots shows altitude, speed and acceleration against time, with a lock strip and satellite count underneath.

SkyTraq PX1125R

SkyTraq binary · conducted · ~70 dB pad + DC block into RF_IN, TX gain 44-47

Textbook behaviour: both export limits enforced independently, velocity at 510–517 m/s and altitude at 80 km, re-opening within 1.5 s whenever four or more satellites were held.

Velocity gate 510-517 m/s  ·  Altitude gate 79.90-80.20 km  ·  Satellites min 2, median 7

u-blox SAM-M10Q

UBX · radiated, Faraday cage · 100 dB pad, L1 quarter-wave, TX gain 12

The flight computer's own receiver, and the tightest data on the bench: never fewer than four satellites in either flight, so every withheld epoch is unambiguously the gate.

Velocity gate 514-516 m/s  ·  Altitude gate ~80.16 km  ·  Satellites min 4, median 13

u-blox ZED-F9P (ArduSimple)

UBX · conducted · 70 dB pad, TX gain 38

Same thresholds as the others, but 2–3 s slow to close the altitude gate — 400–600 m of overshoot above 80 km with position still being published.

Velocity gate 514-518 m/s  ·  Altitude gate 80.22-80.48 km  ·  Satellites min 6, median 13

u-blox NEO-M8T

UBX @ 115200 · conducted · 70 dB pad, TX gain 38

Velocity gate normal at 510–524 m/s, but it stops publishing at 50 km — the u-blox dynamic-model ceiling, not an export limit. Its true altitude behaviour is therefore unmeasurable.

Velocity gate 510-524 m/s  ·  Altitude gate 49.80-50.15 km (dynamic model)  ·  Satellites min 8, median 14

Air530 (AT6558R)

NMEA 0183 @ 9600 · conducted · 70 dB pad, TX gain 32

The outlier. No velocity gate at all, and it stops publishing at 10 km — below every candidate export altitude, and below apogee for most high-power flights.

Velocity gate none to 900 m/s  ·  Altitude gate 10.00-11.00 km (not COCOM)  ·  Satellites min 6, median 12

04Excursion tests

The flight profiles were enough for four of the five parts. They were not enough for the Air530 which, despite not implementing the MTCR velocity limit, it also had the worst performance. Unlike every other unit, the Air530 periodically drops the fix internally during times it is blocked — i.e. above 10 km.

This means that additional scenarios were needed to study the behavior of the unit. So in addition to the data below, other scenarios were also run to confirm the altitude limit and lack of velocity limit.

Excursion scenarios
ScenarioShapeQuestion it answers
vel_stair90 s dwells, 495–530 m/s at 5 kmwhere is the velocity gate, latency removed
alt_stair90 s dwells, 76–82 kmwhere is the altitude gate near 80 km
alt_stair_low90 s dwells, 12–22 kmis there a gate anywhere in the low tens of km
alt_stair_vlow90 s dwells, 8–13 kmbrackets a ceiling below any export limit
blockdur5 / 30 / 150 s excursions, 155 s clear betweenis a slow recovery a gate, or the receiver re-converging

What they established for the Air530

Three tests, three ways of asking the same question, all agreeing there is no velocity gate: 100% of epochs held a fix at every 90 s dwell from 495 to 530 m/s; a ramp to 900 m/s at 5 km never lost the fix and reported 899 m/s against 900 injected; and on blockdur the receiver held a fix at 560 m/s for 148 continuous seconds.

What it has instead is an altitude ceiling at 10–11 km. The dwell staircase is unambiguous — 100% of epochs fixed at 8 km, 97% at 9, 91% at 10, and not one epoch at 11, 12 or 13 km, with ten or eleven satellites tracked throughout — and two independent ramps agree (fix at 9.90 km, blocked at 10.25 km at a constant 354 m/s; fix at 10.10, blocked at 10.44 at 394 m/s).

That ceiling is not an export gate. It sits far below the COCOM altitude, and alt_stair_vlow crosses no export limit at all — 13 km and 156 m/s are well inside the envelope.

On a flight profile the ceiling and the velocity limit fire within moments of each other, because a rocket crosses 10 km while travelling fast. The distinguishing observation is on spaceshot, where the fix stops while speed is falling (1334 → 1304 m/s) as altitude rises through 9.83 km. No velocity gate fires on decreasing speed.

The same trap on the NEO-M8T

The M8T stops publishing at 50 km, which is the documented maximum altitude of u-blox's airborne dynamic models rather than an MTCR limit. The M8T has different models, and changing the model changed the limit, confirming that it was the model driving the limit and not MTCR. For example switching from airborne <4 g to portable moved the same ceiling from 49.80 km to 5.04 km.

No u-blox M8T model exceeds 50 km. The SAM-M10Q and ZED-F9P held fixes to 80 km, so it is an M8-generation behaviour.

05A receiver-side artifact

The Air530's satellite count dips on a tight 18 s cycle. Ruling out bench issues here was important, since loose connectors or other bench artifacts can drive errors. Three tests placed this behavior on the Air530 and not the bench though.

A control part on the same path shows none of it. The ZED-F9P ran the identical scenario files through the identical 70 dB conducted chain with zero periodic dips. Every satellite blanks in the same epoch and returns together within three — attenuation is graded, so a real signal problem takes the weakest first; instead all twelve go from a flat 49 dBHz to an empty C/N₀ field at once, which is a reporting decision, not a level. And it happens while the receiver is withholding: 19 of 677 such epochs on gentle_alt against 0 of 170 while publishing, and on blockdur, where it holds a fix almost throughout, 2 events in 988 epochs.

18 s is three GPS subframes, the span of subframes 1–3 that carry the ephemeris, so the part may re-validate ephemeris on that cadence and blank C/N₀ while doing so. That is a hypothesis; the three observations above stand without it.
